articles.title: Karwa Chauth 2026: Date, puja muhurat, sargi, fasting rules and moonrise rituals — everything you need to know
articles.summary: Karwa Chauth isn’t just another festival; it’s practically woven into the fabric of Indian marital tradition, with millions of families marking the
articles.body: Karwa Chauth isn’t just another festival; it’s practically woven into the fabric of Indian marital tradition, with millions of families marking the occasion every year. In 2026, Karwa Chauth falls on Thursday, October 29. All over India, we’ll see homes decorated, women dressed in vibrant outfits, and elders passing on rituals that have survived generations. The day of Karwa Chauth isn’t just about fasting; it’s about love, dedication, and the hope for a long, happy married life. It’s the kind of festival where the smallest details matter, from the pre-dawn meal to that magical moment when the Moon finally peeks through the night sky.Karwa Chauth: What exactly is it?First of all, it falls on the fourth day (Chaturthi) of the Krishna Paksha, which is the waning phase of the Moon in the Hindu lunar calendar. Married women, mainly Hindu, observe a strict fast for their husbands’ well-being. The meaning behind it runs deep: devotion, companionship, and a prayer for longevity. But every household puts its own spin on the customs, with some sticking strictly to tradition and others tweaking things to fit more modern lifestyles.This year, there’s been a bit of confusion, as some calendars mention October 28, but if you check the lunar calculations, it falls on October 29. The difference is important because Karwa Chauth isn’t tied to a set date in the regular calendar. The festival’s timing depends on the right lunar phase lining up with the prescribed hours for fasting and those all-important Moon rituals. In other words, a mix-up can throw off the entire festival’s rhythm.Karwa Chauth 2026: Date, tithi, and puja muhuratFor 2026, Karwa Chauth is observed on October 29. According to the Panchang, Chaturthi tithi starts at 1:06 am and wraps up at 10:09 pm. In New Delhi, the most auspicious puja time runs from 5:38 pm to 6:56 pm, but you should check your local Panchang: timings for sunrise, sunset, and moonrise can change quite a bit from city to city. Preparing ahead makes the day go a lot smoother.Now, Karwa Chauth is usually dedicated to Goddess Parvati, worshipped as Karwa Mata or Chauth Mata, depending on your family tradition. Sometimes prayers include Lord Shiva, Lord Ganesha, and Lord Kartikeya as well. The rituals are all about blessings, hoping for a happy marriage, a prosperous family, and long, healthy lives.Sargi: The meal that starts Karwa ChauthBefore dawn, women have sargi. It’s not just a meal; it’s a tradition, especially in North India. Mothers-in-law typically prepare or gift sargi to their daughters-in-law, packing it with fruits, dry fruits, sweets, nuts, and sometimes home-cooked favorites. Milk-based dishes and regional goodies often show up, too. The food isn’t just for nutrition; it’s a symbol that connects women in the family, reminding everyone of the support behind the fast.Alongside sargi, there’s baya, which includes gifts from a woman’s parents, including sweets, clothes, cosmetics, and other treats. Once sargi is eaten, the fast begins. Most women observe a strict nirjala vrat: no food, no water. It’s tough, and not everyone follows it the same way. Some modify the fast depending on their health or family custom.Karwa Chauth rituals: Puja thali, mehendi, and the vrat kathaAs evening arrives, homes buzz with preparation. Women slip into festive outfits, often red, pink, or the brightest shade their wardrobe offers. Mehendi is a must, with each hand painted with intricate designs. The puja thali sits at the center of it all, holding a diya, roli or kumkum, rice grains, flowers, sweets, and of course, the karwa (an earthen pot).The evening brings prayers to Goddess Parvati and other deities, carried out according to family and regional customs. One universal element is the Karwa Chauth vrat katha, a story that lends meaning to the fast. The story of Veeravati is the most popular, where her brothers trick her into breaking her fast early, and her husband suffers the consequences. Through devotion, she wins him back. It’s a tale reminding everyone not to cut corners, and while most know this version, each community might tell it a little differently.Many women join together for the puja, trading thalis, singing traditional songs, and sharing the katha. The gathering isn’t just about rituals; it’s a social ceremony, affirming community bonds and celebrating shared heritage.Moonrise: The end of the fast and the start of celebrationThe Moonrise is the highlight of Karwa Chauth. As soon as it’s visible, women view the Moon through a sieve, offer water as arghya, and pray for their husband’s well-being. Then, they look at their husbands through the sieve, who often hand them water or a sweet to break the fast. Every home has its own sequence, but the Moon ceremony is always the heart of the festival.The karwa, which is the little pot, plays a special role in the offering. Moonrise times differ by city, so make sure that you check for your own city timings.Breaking the fast comes after the Moon has been sighted and worshipped. There’s a sense of accomplishment, relief, and celebration, as families gather, share sweets, and enjoy a meal together.Things to keep in mindGetting ready for Karwa Chauth means planning the puja, checking local timings, and sticking to your family’s traditions. No two families do everything exactly the same. Importantly, fasting without water is demanding. So, if you’re pregnant, nursing, diabetic, or on medication, it’s best to check with a doctor first. Health always comes before ritual.Moreover, Karwa Chauth has changed over time. It used to be just women fasting for their husbands. Now, some couples fast together, flipping the tradition and making it more about mutual love and support. It’s a sign that families adapt rituals to fit their own beliefs and relationships.At its core, Karwa Chauth is about faith, tradition, and the thrill of spotting the Moon after a challenging day. From the early-morning sargi to the late-night prayers, it’s a celebration of love, family, and enduring customs that still mean everything to so many across India.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Needle exchange: Vulnerable at risk as 'life-saving' drug needle site closes
articles.summary: Belfast charity workers warn people who use the "life-saving" service will be left without support.
articles.body:
A drug needle exchange in Belfast is set to close within days because the charity which runs the service is losing its city centre premises.

The exchange, run by Extern, allowed people who inject heroin or cocaine to safely dispose used needles, receive clean needles and access health services.

The service will shut on 2 November and move to a "significantly reduced street-based service" following the loss of Extern's Royal Avenue premises.

The charity described the needle exchange as a "life-saving service" and warned that its closure meant vulnerable people would have "nowhere to go" to access support.

"The people who use this service are someone's son, daughter, brother, sister, parent or friend," said Mal Byrne, Extern's director of harm reduction and mental health services.

"They are members of our community, and, for many, this service is one of the few places where the door is open for them and where they can ask for help without judgement.

"That door is now closed until a space is secured to operate from."

Extern has also warned that the closure may mean substance use becomes more visible to the public in the city centre, along with an increase in drug-related litter.

The charity's premises is to be redeveloped as part of the Belfast Stories project and Extern has tried for more than a year to find an alternative site in the city centre.

The search was assisted by Belfast City Council, the Public Health Agency (PHA), the Department of Health and landlords but a new location is yet to be found.

In addition to clean needles, the exchange provided a wound-dressing service and advised the vulnerable about accessing temporary accommodation and healthcare.

"Loss of a premises means people who need support to reduce harms from substance use have nowhere to go to access life-saving harm reduction advice and interventions, healthcare support and wider practical assistance," Byrne said.

"This is a life-saving service. This work will be suspended."

The forthcoming closure is happening at a time when cocaine use is believed to be on the rise in Belfast city centre, according to Extern.

"We suspect that there are between 1,000 and 1,500 people at any one-time experiencing difficulties with their drug use," the charity said.

"Last year alone, almost 20,000 used needles were safely returned by individuals who came to the premises on Royal Avenue," it added.

"Extern's city centre outreach team removed more than 13,000 discarded needles from Belfast's streets.

"This is an increase of roughly 20% from previous years."

A service user said going to the exchange was not just about exchanging needles but also the people who work there.

"Over the last number of years, I've built up a bond with a couple of the workers," they said.

Adding that there are days when they go in "feeling very low, not going in to use equipment, but just to go in to get a chat".

Speaking about the impact the closure will have on their mental health they described their lifestyle as lonely and isolating and said the people at Extern "become like family".

"You kind of hold them close, it will have a big impact with our mental health with this going."

Independent councillor Paul McCusker warned the closure puts vulnerable people "at even greater risk" and he has lobbied the council to explore alternative locations.

"I am deeply concerned that any reduction in this service will have a devastating impact on the people who rely upon it," he said.

"I have known individuals who have suffered life-changing consequences as a result of addiction, including the loss of limbs, and sadly, the loss of life itself.

"Belfast is currently in the midst of a drug epidemic, yet the political response has not reflected the scale of the crisis."

McCusker founded a soup kitchen in north Belfast in 2017 and regularly campaigns on issues regarding homelessness, poverty and addiction.

"Over recent years, we have witnessed a substantial increase in the number of people injecting drugs, which has led to an increased risk of blood-borne viruses, serious infections, abscesses, and addiction-related health complications," he said.

McCusker added needle exchange services "play a vital role in reducing harm" and insisted the "fears and misconceptions" surrounding them must be challenged.

"They provide an opportunity for drug support workers to engage with individuals, build trust, minimise health risks, and ensure that those who need help can be referred to appropriate treatment and support services."

The PHA commissions charities and participating pharmacies to deliver the Enhanced Needle and Syringe Exchange Service (NSES) across Northern Ireland.

In 2024-2025, a total of 32,667 transactions were recorded by the NSES in Northern Ireland, an increase of 7.4% on the year before.

About 721,000 needles and syringes were given out, which is a 7.5% increase compared with the previous year.

The PHA said needle exchange sites "are located in areas where there is an existing pattern of injecting behaviour"

"Providing services locally is vital, as people who inject substances are often vulnerable, may be in poor health, can be dealing with complex social issues, and may be without local access to sterile equipment and advice.

"So support needs to be targeted in a way which maximises access.

"Needle exchanges are particularly valuable for engaging these people, because it may be the only service they are willing to use and provides opportunities to direct them to additional support and information," the PHA added.

articles.title: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
articles.summary: The troops are trying to recover four military personnel who went missing in an ambush on the outskirts of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince.
articles.body:
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.

The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.

Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.

Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.

The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.

No gang has so far claimed responsibility.

The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".

Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.

He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.

Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.

In October last year , the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.

Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

articles.title: As Trump mulls fresh strikes after midterms, Vance writes to Iran, Tehran says 'won't surrender'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Iran is pursuing a seven-day plan to secure a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as diplomatic efforts intensify amid the possibility of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Iran is pursuing a seven-day plan to secure a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as diplomatic efforts intensify amid the possibility of renewed US military strikes after the November 3 midterm elections. US Vice President JD Vance has reportedly reached out to Iran’s security leadership to explore a framework for negotiations, even as Washington warns Gulf allies to prepare for a potential escalation.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that Tehran was working with regional mediators to advance the proposal, which Iran had previously conveyed to the United States through Qatar. He said the plan could be implemented in less than a week if the necessary conditions were met."While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi said in a post on X."We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."The proposal dates back to September, when the Iranian delegation was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It has resurfaced following recent diplomatic engagements in the region, particularly Qatar's involvement, according to Al Jazeera's reporting from Tehran.An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera that the plan was not fundamentally new. Tehran has also indicated that the seven-day period could be shortened, suggesting that the central question is whether Iran's demands and conditions can be met.Under the proposal, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen within seven days if conditions, including a ceasefire across the Middle East, were fulfilled. Iran has also demanded the unfreezing of its assets held abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.Vance contacts Iran's security chief as Washington explores talksThe diplomatic push comes as The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance had sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in an effort to revive negotiations and avert renewed American attacks.The report said the contact was made at the direction of US President Donald Trump. The letter and subsequent discussions between US and Iranian officials focused on exploring a framework for negotiations rather than the details of a comprehensive peace proposal.Separately, US news website Axios reported that regional mediators led by Qatar were pushing for an agreement to restart US-Iran talks and prevent a resumption of hostilities after the November 3 US midterm elections.Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch fresh strikes against Iran, according to diplomats briefed on the matter and cited by The Associated Press (AP).Washington has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the elections, The Wall Street Journal reported. US officials have also urged regional allies to prepare for potential Iranian retaliation against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure.Iran warns of economic fallout from renewed attacksTehran has warned that renewed military action could have far-reaching consequences for global energy markets, particularly if fighting disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.“Devastating impact on int’l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Arabian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers,” Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.The Strait of Hormuz is a critical shipping route through which around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies previously passed. Iran has restricted maritime traffic through the waterway since the war began in late February and has attacked vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.The United States, meanwhile, has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports to put pressure on Tehran's economy.Iran has warned that any renewed attack would trigger a broader response. Rezaei has threatened strikes against US-linked infrastructure, including data centres and facilities associated with artificial intelligence.Concerns over the safety of American personnel have also intensified. In a memo dated October 23 and reviewed by Reuters, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran had stepped up efforts to target American personnel and that alleged plots against US citizens had reached advanced stages."Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added.Trump keeps military option open ahead of midtermsTrump has repeatedly suggested that the conflict could end soon while keeping open the possibility of renewed bombing after the November 3 elections.During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the conflict could come “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”“Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.”The conflict has become a political challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms, with rising petrol prices adding to voter concerns about its economic consequences. The Pentagon's latest estimate to Congress put the cost of the war to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion.The military situation has also become more complicated as the conflict has spread across the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have attacked Saudi oil infrastructure and airports, while a Saudi-led coalition has carried out strikes against Houthi-held territory in Yemen.The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry has urged the parties to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale military operations.Mojtaba Khamenei calls for end to 'neither war nor peace' situationIran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei has called for an end to the region's state of 'neither war nor peace', as Tehran prepares for the possibility of renewed military confrontation with the United States and Israel.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the country's cabinet on Wednesday that the government would pursue the implementation of the supreme leader's directive with full commitment and resources, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.The Iranian cabinet discussed the country's prevailing conditions, strengthening national resilience and countering external threats. Pezeshkian stressed the need for continuous preparedness to deal with different possible scenarios."All ministers, heads and deputies of the executive branches are obliged to maintain full readiness based on requirements, and use the existing capacities to increase productivity and strengthen the national power," he said.Pezeshkian also called for greater resilience against threats, sanctions and external pressure."Enemies should not think they can weaken the will of the Iranian nation and force the country to surrender," he stressed.During the meeting, Araghchi briefed the cabinet on diplomatic developments and regional consultations, particularly those involving a visiting Qatari delegation and Pakistan's army chief.The remarks come as Tehran pursues diplomatic efforts to revive negotiations while preparing for a possible confrontation. Vance's reported outreach to Rezaei and the proposed seven-day plan indicate that diplomatic channels remain active, even as Washington keeps the military option open.Whether the proposal can meet Iran's demands, secure a ceasefire and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains uncertain as the November 3 US midterm elections approach.You use AI every day. articles.title: Venezuela's 2016 bond deal put 50.1% of US oil refiner Citgo's parent up as security, now a US appeals court has rejected its bid to void the debt as a separate sale plan earmarks over $2 billion for the bonds
articles.summary: A US federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld the validity of bonds issued by Venezuela’s state-owned oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) that
articles.body: A US federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld the validity of bonds issued by Venezuela’s state-owned oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) that defaulted in 2019, ruling that the transaction did not require prior approval from the country’s National Assembly.The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a lower court judgment that found the bonds enforceable under Venezuelan law. The ruling is significant because the bonds are secured by a 50.1% equity interest in CITGO Holding, the parent company of US oil refiner CITGO Petroleum, potentially allowing creditors to pursue the collateral to recover their dues.The decision follows a prolonged legal dispute over whether PDVSA had the constitutional authority to issue the bonds without legislative approval. The company and related entities had sought to have the transaction declared void, arguing that it violated Venezuela’s Constitution.The bonds traded flat on Tuesday at 114.25 cents on the dollar.The case centres on a 2016 bond exchange through which holders of PDVSA’s unsecured notes due in 2017 could exchange them for new, secured notes due in 2020. PDVSA offered the exchange as its financial position deteriorated following a significant fall in crude oil prices between 2014 and 2016.Holders representing about 39.4% of the outstanding principal on the earlier notes accepted the offer. In return, the new bonds were secured by a 50.1% equity interest in CITGO Holding, which PDVSA owned through a chain of subsidiaries.PDVSA’s board approved the exchange in September 2016, along with the relevant approvals from the Venezuelan government as its sole shareholder and the boards of its subsidiaries involved in the transaction.However, Venezuela’s National Assembly, then controlled by opposition parties, challenged the arrangement. It argued that Article 150 of the Venezuelan Constitution required legislative approval for national public interest contracts involving foreign companies.The assembly passed resolutions in 2016 rejecting the use of CITGO shares as collateral and, in October 2019, reiterated that the bond agreement violated the Constitution. PDVSA subsequently failed to make scheduled principal and interest payments on the 2020 notes in October 2019, triggering the dispute.PDVSA, its subsidiary PDVSA Petróleo and holding company PDV Holding argued that the bond exchange and the pledge of CITGO shares were invalid because the National Assembly had not authorised the transaction. They also contended that the assembly’s resolutions should be recognised by US courts under the act-of-state doctrine, which can prevent courts from questioning certain official acts of foreign sovereigns.The US District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favour of the creditors in September 2025. It concluded that the transaction was valid under Venezuelan law and that the act-of-state doctrine did not apply.The Second Circuit upheld that judgment. In examining Venezuelan constitutional law, the appeals court relied on interpretations by Venezuela’s Constitutional Chamber indicating that national public interest contracts requiring legislative approval are those entered into by the Republic or competent organs of the National Executive. PDVSA, as a state-owned enterprise within the country’s decentralised public administration, did not fall within that category, the court concluded.The appeals court also agreed that the act-of-state doctrine did not invalidate the transaction. It noted that the relevant agreements were executed in the United States, payments were due in New York and the collateral was held there. The doctrine’s territorial limitation therefore prevented its application to the dispute, the court said.The ruling strengthens the creditors’ position in their efforts to enforce the bonds and recover money owed following PDVSA’s default. However, the judgment does not mean that the creditors can immediately take control of the pledged CITGO shares.The case forms part of broader litigation over PDVSA’s ownership interests in CITGO and other claims against Venezuela. A separate proceeding in Delaware concerns the proposed sale of PDV Holding, which owns CITGO Holding. A court-approved plan for the sale and resolution of creditor claims commits more than $2 billion towards extinguishing at least two-thirds of the 2020 notes, according to the Second Circuit’s opinion.The approval of that sale remains under appeal in the Third Circuit. US sanctions have also constrained creditors’ ability to execute against the CITGO shares without the necessary authorisation.The Second Circuit’s decision resolves the appeal over the validity of the 2020 notes, while enforcement and recovery remain subject to the separate proceedings and applicable restrictions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Google billionaire's wife Wendy Schmidt launched a $1.4 million challenge after the Deepwater Horizon disaster, inviting scientists and engineers to develop faster oil-cleanup technology; one winning device recovered 4,670 gallons per minute
articles.summary: After the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill devastated the Gulf of Mexico, philanthropist Wendy Schmidt launched a $1.4 million challenge to find faster
articles.body: After the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill devastated the Gulf of Mexico, philanthropist Wendy Schmidt launched a $1.4 million challenge to find faster and more efficient ways to remove oil from the ocean. The wife of former Google CEO Eric Schmidt funded the Wendy Schmidt Oil Cleanup XCHALLENGE, inviting engineers, scientists and companies to develop technologies that could outperform conventional oil-recovery equipment.The competition attracted more than 350 entries from around the world, with finalists testing their inventions under controlled conditions designed to simulate real-world oil spills. One team, Elastec/American Marine, developed a skimmer that recovered oil at a rate of 4,670 gallons per minute, achieving 89.5% efficiency. The competition demonstrated how financial incentives could encourage innovation in a field where existing technology had struggled to keep pace with the demands of major environmental disasters.Wendy Schmidt launched a $1.4 million oil-cleanup challengeThe Deepwater Horizon disaster began on April 20, 2010, when an explosion aboard an offshore drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers. The subsequent oil spill became one of the largest environmental disasters in US history, releasing millions of barrels of oil into the sea and threatening marine wildlife, coastal habitats and communities dependent on the Gulf.The disaster also exposed the limitations of existing oil-spill response technology. Conventional skimmers, which collect oil from the surface of the water, could struggle to recover large quantities quickly and efficiently. The scale of the spill highlighted the need for equipment capable of removing oil faster while limiting the amount of water collected alongside it.Against this backdrop, Wendy Schmidt funded the Oil Cleanup XCHALLENGE, organised by the XPRIZE Foundation in 2010. The competition aimed to accelerate technological development by offering substantial financial rewards to teams that could demonstrate significant improvements in oil recovery.What the Wendy Schmidt Oil Cleanup XCHALLENGE demandedThe competition set a demanding target for participants: develop technology capable of recovering more than 2,500 gallons of oil per minute, with an efficiency of at least 70%.The goal was to encourage solutions that could operate at substantially higher recovery rates than conventional equipment. Teams had to demonstrate that their systems could remove oil from the water's surface without collecting excessive amounts of water alongside it.More than 350 submissions came from teams around the world. Ten finalists progressed to testing at OHMSETT, the US government's National Oil Spill Response Research and Renewable Energy Test Facility in New Jersey.The facility allowed the competing teams to test their equipment in controlled conditions designed to replicate aspects of oil-spill response at sea. The trials provided a common basis for comparing the technologies' recovery rates and efficiency.How one team developed a skimmer that recovered 4,670 gallons per minuteThe winning entry came from Elastec/American Marine, an environmental equipment company with operations in Illinois and Florida. Its technology, known as the Grooved Disc Skimmer, used rotating plastic discs to separate oil from water.The design relied on a relatively simple principle. Oil adheres to the grooved surfaces of the discs, while much less water sticks to them. As the discs rotate, the collected oil is scraped off and pumped away for recovery.The concept built on the company's earlier work developing oil-skimming equipment. Its founders, Donnie Wilson and Jeff Cantrell, had previously explored ways to improve oil recovery after encountering problems with equipment that collected too much water.During the XCHALLENGE trials, the system achieved an average oil recovery rate of 4,670 gallons per minute, with an oil recovery efficiency of 89.5%. Its performance exceeded the competition's minimum targets and established a significant benchmark for the technology tested.How much money did the winning team receive?The competition offered a total prize purse of $1.4 million, with the largest award going to Elastec/American Marine.The winning team received $1 million for its Grooved Disc Skimmer. Norway-based NOFI secured second place and received $300,000 after achieving an average recovery rate of 2,712 gallons per minute and an efficiency of 83%.The awards were announced in October 2011, following the testing programme. The results showed that both teams had exceeded the competition's minimum targets, with Elastec/American Marine delivering the strongest performance.The prize was designed not simply to reward an invention but to encourage the development of equipment that could be manufactured and used beyond the competition.What happened to the winning technology after the competition?Elastec continued developing its oil-recovery equipment after winning the challenge. The company adapted the technology into commercial skimmers, including the X150, designed for oil-spill response applications.The company's equipment portfolio includes oil skimmers, containment booms and other environmental products used to manage pollution in waterways and marine environments. Its products are distributed internationally.The XCHALLENGE gave the company an opportunity to demonstrate its technology under independently assessed testing conditions and helped bring greater attention to its design. The experience also showed how a competition with a clear performance target could help move an existing concept towards wider commercial application.How Wendy Schmidt's challenge sought to change oil-spill responseThe Oil Cleanup XCHALLENGE was part of a broader approach to philanthropy that uses financial incentives to encourage technical innovation. Rather than directing funding towards a single research team, the competition invited participants from different backgrounds to develop and test their own solutions against a common target.The approach gave established companies and other innovators an opportunity to compete on demonstrated performance. It also created a measurable way to assess progress in a field where the speed and efficiency of equipment can affect the response to an environmental emergency.The winning technology's performance established a benchmark during the competition, while subsequent commercial development helped extend its reach beyond the original trials.You use AI every day. articles.title: Theni jailbreak puts spotlight on overcrowded Tamil Nadu prisons
articles.summary: The jailbreak began with a fake seizure and ended 36 hours later with all the inmates back behind bars.
articles.body:
A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.

Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.

It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.

The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.

The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.

All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.

On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.

The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.

Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.

Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.

Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".

"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.

At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.

The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.

"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.

Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.

A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.

Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.

News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.

Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.

The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.

While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.

Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.

Additional reporting by Siraj and Prabhurao Anandhan

articles.title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.summary: All but one of England's water companies were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement" for environmental targets.
articles.body:
The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.

Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.

Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".

The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".

"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".

Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.

It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation .

But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.

Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.

Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".

And in Wales, Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.

Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".

But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".

"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.

Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".

And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.

Will record investment deliver improvement?

Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average between 2025 and 2030 as a result.

There has already been £5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution.

But Alan Lovell from the EA said: "Not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for."

In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.

Mike Keil, chief executive of the CCW, said that "many customers have not noticed any improvement in customer service or performance" despite recent bill rises.

"People support investment and understand it takes time to bear fruit," he said, but added that "bill payers are already questioning whether their money is being well spent".

The government is planning to introduce new legislation next year to overhaul the structure and regulation of the industry - including combining the regulators in England.

The Welsh government plans to set up a new regulator alongside Natural Resources Wales.

In his Labour conference speech last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a strengthened Water Bill would also remove limits on government ownership of shares in England's major water companies.

He also promised new powers for local leaders . The BBC understands further details on the idea of "regional bodies" to oversee water companies are likely to follow in the coming weeks.

Water consumption fails to fall, risking supplies

The joint report, published on Thursday, also found that household consumption in England and Wales in 2025 remained similar to the previous year, at 137 litres per person per day.

Government advisers have said that demand for water will likely have to fall to safeguard future supplies , which are facing pressures from climate change, a growing population and historic underinvestment.

Hosepipe bans remain in place across large parts of England and Wales as companies have sought to shore up supplies following drought this summer.

Mark Owen, head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said the industry also needed to take more responsibility and cut leakage rates further.

"Every litre lost has already been taken from the environment while our rivers, fish and wildlife are under immense pressure," he said.

articles.title: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
articles.summary: The term "associate member" is reportedly off the table as officials discuss deeper economic and defence ties.
articles.body:
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.

Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.

The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".

Von der Leyen, speaking to reporters after landing in Montreal on Wednesday, said the two sides will "start discussing how to make Canada the first associate member of the EU".

"Our ambition is to build the closest partnership we have ever had with a non-European country," she said.

Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.

Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.

According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".

Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.

The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.

"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.

Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.

Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.

On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.

Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.

Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.

But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.

Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.

And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.

"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.

What could EU associate member status mean for Canada?

Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'

Many Canadians are boycotting the US, so this is where they're travelling instead

Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.

US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".

Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.

Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.

It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.

Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.

As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.

"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

articles.title: Israel polls: Poll chief orders probe into 'foreign interference'; Netanyahu levels big charge - top developments
articles.summary: Israel’s election chief has ordered a probe into alleged foreign interference in the October 28 election.
articles.body: Israel’s election chief has ordered a probe into alleged foreign interference in the October 28 election.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-led parties of stealing the vote and warned of a foreign takeover of parliament.The allegations emerged on Thursday as final results were awaited and neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition had secured a clear path to a majority in the 120-member Knesset.Israel's central elections committee chair, Justice Noam Sohlberg, asked Shin Bet chief David Zini to investigate suspicions of improper influence through foreign funding and alleged electoral bribery. Sohlberg said he could not confirm the validity of the claims but called for a thorough investigation. He asked Zini to submit findings within a week.Poll chief orders probe into alleged foreign interferenceSohlberg directed the Shin Bet to investigate allegations that foreign entities had sought to influence the election through funding.In his letter to Zini, he wrote, “Serious suspicions have been brought to my attention regarding improper influence on the elections — exerted through funding provided by foreign entities acting against Israeli interests.”He added, “While I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions, it is my view that — given they involve foreign entities — there is an obligation to investigate them thoroughly.”Sohlberg said the Shin Bet should use its authority to establish whether evidence supported or refuted the allegations. He called the investigation necessary to protect public confidence in the electoral process and democratic institutions.The allegations have not been independently established. Sohlberg did not identify the countries allegedly involved or provide further details about the suspected interference.Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of stealing electionsNetanyahu seized on the investigation to intensify his attack on Arab-led parties and oppose any attempt by his rivals to form a government with their support.In a post on X, he said, “The Ra'amgate affair is an earthquake. They stole the elections in Israel!”He added: “This is an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to lead to retreat and defeat of the IDF in all arenas - and primarily Iran.”Netanyahu also called for immediate action by the security agency and police. “We demand to act immediately and with all means available to the Shin Bet and the police to investigate these crimes,” he said.Likud has argued that the allegations should rule out cooperation between Zionist parties and the Arab-led Ra’am and Joint List parties. It warned against forming a government with their support or replacing the Knesset speaker through what it described as votes bought with cash.The accusations remain claims made by Netanyahu and his party. Police have previously said there was “no supporting evidence” for Likud’s allegation that Arab-led parties stole the election.Likud suspects Qatar and Turkey behind alleged fundingNetanyahu’s Likud party suspects Qatar and Turkey may have funded get-out-the-vote groups targeting Arab citizens in Israel, according to Hebrew-language media reports.Channel 12 reported that the investigation was based on intelligence received by the Shin Bet and presented to Sohlberg. The reports said the channels allegedly used to transfer money to the organisations closely resembled those previously used to send funds for terrorism.However, the alleged involvement of Qatar and Turkey has not been established. Sohlberg did not identify any country as being behind the suspected interference.The allegations have taken on greater political significance because Arab-led parties could help Netanyahu’s opponents secure a majority. The investigation could therefore influence the debate over whether opposition parties should cooperate with them to form a government.Four arrested in alleged voter bribery caseFour men were arrested on Thursday and were being questioned by the Lahav 433 major crimes unit over an alleged voter bribery scheme, Israeli police said.The arrests followed the detention of three southern Bedouin men on election day, Tuesday, on suspicion of planning to pay people to vote for Ra’am.Ra’am has identified the men as party activists and denied the allegations. It remains unclear whether the arrests are connected to the Shin Bet’s investigation into suspected foreign interference.The separate bribery case has added to the political controversy surrounding the election. However, the arrests do not by themselves establish that the alleged scheme took place or that foreign actors were involved.Neither Netanyahu nor opposition has a clear majorityThe election has left Israel facing a difficult coalition-building process. Local media projections put Netanyahu’s bloc at 53 seats, opposition parties at 48 and Arab-led parties at 19 in the 120-member Knesset.A party or bloc needs at least 61 seats to secure a parliamentary majority. Neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition can currently reach that threshold on their own.The Arab-led parties could therefore play a decisive role in determining the next government, even if they do not join a formal coalition.Netanyahu’s Likud party has received the most votes, but that does not automatically guarantee him another term. The president traditionally asks the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government, although this is not a legal requirement.Eisenkot open to cooperation with Arab-led partiesNetanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has said he is open to working with Arab-led parties to reach the 61-seat threshold.Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint List, told Army Radio that the opposition bloc had approached him about replacing the Knesset speaker. He said his party would support the bloc’s candidate and urged Eisenkot to show political courage.The Joint List described the election result as an “unprecedented show of strength” by Arab voters and praised Jewish voters “willing to swim against the tide of racism.”Small rallies were held overnight in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties.Such cooperation would be politically significant. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined an Israeli coalition government. The brief participation of an Arab party in a coalition that year marked a historic departure.Netanyahu’s party is seeking to use the foreign interference allegations to discourage such an arrangement. The opposition, meanwhile, faces the challenge of building a majority without abandoning its central campaign pledge to remove him from power.Final results expected after absentee ballots are countedFinal election results could come as early as Thursday evening, once around half a million absentee ballots have been counted. The ballots include votes from military personnel, diplomats, prisoners, hospital patients and others.The votes are not expected to alter the overall result dramatically, according to the available projections.Israel’s election results must be certified by November 4. President Isaac Herzog is expected to task someone with forming the next government the following week.The swearing-in of the new parliament is scheduled for November 10. Eisenkot has warned political actors against using the investigation to influence the timing of the process.If coalition negotiations fail after multiple attempts, Israel could face another election early next year. Herzog has indicated that he wants to avoid that outcome.Political deadlock comes amid deep divisionsThe election has exposed divisions over security, religion and the future direction of Israel.One major issue is whether the fast-growing ultra-Orthodox population should continue to be exempt from compulsory military service. The question has become more contentious after three years of inconclusive wars and military losses.Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains a polarising figure. He faces corruption allegations and accusations that he delayed a deal to secure the release of hostages held in Gaza for political gain.Israel’s international standing is also at stake following widespread criticism of its treatment of Palestinians in Gaza and growing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank.Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population. Their stronger electoral showing has raised hopes among some voters that Arab-led parties could gain greater influence over government policy and parliamentary decisions.“God willing, we will have something for us in the government, something that will bring us our rights,” said Brosli Elias, a resident of Nazareth.Possible renewed conflict with Iran adds uncertaintyThe possibility of further strikes against Iran could complicate Israel’s political situation. The Trump administration has spoken of new attacks after the US midterm elections on November 3.Experts have suggested that Netanyahu could use a renewed, large-scale conflict to push for a national unity government under his leadership.Such a development could also delay calls for a public inquiry into the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, the deadliest extremist attack in Israel’s history, which triggered the war in Gaza.For now, the election investigation, the unresolved parliamentary arithmetic and the dispute over cooperation with Arab-led parties are likely to shape the next phase of government formation. The central question is whether Netanyahu can remain in power or whether his opponents can assemble a viable alternative.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From Hitler’s rise to farmers’ misery in India: How the Great Depression changed lives far beyond America
articles.summary: In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond
articles.body: In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond Wall Street.Years of speculative buying, easy credit and inflated share prices had created a market built on the expectation that stocks would keep rising. When confidence collapsed, investors rushed to sell. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged nearly 13 per cent on October 28 and another 12 per cent the following day, in what became known as Black Monday and Black Tuesday.But the crash was only the beginning. Bank failures, collapsing demand and business closures deepened the American downturn, while the withdrawal of US loans, falling international trade and the constraints of the gold standard carried the crisis across borders.The result was the Great Depression, a global disaster that would help propel Adolf Hitler towards power in Germany, devastate farmers in colonial India, push millions of Britons into unemployment, and expose the fragility of economies around the world.What followed was not merely a financial collapse, but a decade of economic hardship and political upheaval that changed the course of the twentieth century.Germany’s economic collapse turned Hitler into a political forceThe Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe. The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923.Its recovery during the second half of the 1920s depended heavily on foreign credit, particularly loans from the United States.Under the Dawes Plan of 1924, American lending helped stabilise German finances and supported economic recovery. But this dependence became a major weakness when the Wall Street crash struck in October 1929.As American banks and investors came under pressure, new lending dried up and foreign creditors recalled short-term loans. German banks and businesses struggled to obtain credit, investment declined and companies began cutting production and jobs.The consequences were severe. Industrial output contracted, businesses failed and unemployment soared. By 1932, around 5.6 million Germans were registered as unemployed, while industrial production had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from its 1928 level.The crisis also paralysed political decision-making. Chancellor Hermann Müller’s coalition government collapsed in March 1930 amid disagreements over unemployment insurance, paving the way for increasingly unstable governments that relied on presidential emergency powers.This economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. They portrayed the Weimar Republic as weak and incapable of protecting ordinary Germans, promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. Their message appealed to sections of the middle class, struggling farmers, small business owners and workers disillusioned with the political establishment.The electoral shift was dramatic. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazis won just 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 parliamentary election. Their share rose to 18 per cent in September 1930 and 37 per cent in July 1932, making them the largest party in the Reichstag.Nazi campaigning deliberately exploited the hardship. A 1932 election poster preserved by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum carried the slogan “Our Last Hope - Hitler”, presenting the Nazi leader as an answer to national despair.The party used mass rallies, newspapers, posters and speeches to promise economic recovery and political order. At the same time, it spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, blamed Jews and communists for Germany’s problems, and attacked democratic institutions.Hitler did not win an outright majority in a free national election. On January 30, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him chancellor following negotiations with conservative political leaders who believed they could control him. The Nazis subsequently dismantled democracy and established a dictatorship.The Great Depression did not, by itself, cause Hitler’s rise. But the collapse of American lending, mass unemployment and the failure of Germany’s political leadership to restore confidence created conditions that the Nazis exploited with devastating consequences.India’s farmers were crushed as crop prices collapsedIn British-ruled India, the Great Depression turned a global economic crisis into a rural emergency, exposing the financial vulnerability of millions of cultivators and deepening resentment against colonial rule.As international demand weakened and agricultural prices plunged, farmers earned less from their crops but continued to face debts, rent and land revenue obligations. For many, the crisis meant selling produce at a loss, struggling to repay moneylenders and risking the loss of their land.A 2022 research paper by historian Alok Oak, published in Studies in Indian Politics, documents the scale of the collapse. India’s agricultural price index fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, using 1873 as the base year. The price index for raw cotton dropped from 133 to 70 over the same period. The decline was particularly damaging for cultivators who depended on commercial crops to generate cash for household expenses, rent and taxes.The crisis was compounded by the structure of the colonial economy. According to Oak, the British government refused to devalue the rupee amid concerns about meeting its foreign financial obligations. Meanwhile, Britain’s exports to India fell from £90.6 million in 1924 to £52.9 million in 1930, a decline of about 41 per cent. Falling trade and agricultural prices squeezed rural incomes and weakened economic activity.The timing was significant for India’s independence movement. At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its goal. On January 26, 1930, Congress observed Independence Day, building momentum for a new phase of resistance.The Depression did not create the struggle against British rule, which had much deeper roots, but worsening economic conditions made questions of taxation, rural livelihoods and control over India’s economy more urgent.Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, beginning with the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi. By challenging the British monopoly on salt and the tax imposed on a basic necessity, Gandhi chose an issue that affected Indians across social and economic divisions. The campaign transformed an everyday grievance into an act of mass resistance and helped bring the nationalist movement into the lives of ordinary people.Gandhi also urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, particularly British-made cloth, and promoted khadi and domestic production. These campaigns had a political and economic purpose. Reducing dependence on imported goods could challenge British commercial interests while encouraging Indians to support local producers. At a time when the global crisis had exposed the vulnerability of export-dependent economies, the message of economic self-reliance gained added significanceResearch by Stanford University political scientists Rikhil Bhavnani and Saumitra Jha has also identified a link between economic shocks and nationalist mobilisation. Their working paper found that districts producing export crops and affected by interwar trade shocks, including the Depression, were more likely to support the independence movement in the 1937 and 1946 elections.The researchers argue that these shocks helped bring agricultural exporters into a broader coalition demanding political change. The findings suggest that the Depression’s political consequences extended beyond immediate protests and influenced support for nationalism in subsequent years.The crisis also reinforced Gandhi’s emphasis on village industries and economic self-reliance. He argued that political freedom would mean little if rural India remained trapped in poverty and dependent on external markets. Gandhi promoted khadi and cottage industries as ways to create employment, strengthen village economies and reduce dependence on imported goods.In 1934, the All-India Village Industries Association was established to advance this wider effort. Historian Alok Oak argues that the Depression and the limits of colonial economic policy helped strengthen Gandhi’s focus on rural production and economic autonomy.Britain’s industrial decline pushed millions out of workBritain entered the Great Depression with its traditional industries already struggling to compete in international markets. Coal mining, shipbuilding, iron and textiles faced declining demand and growing competition, leaving industrial communities vulnerable when the Wall Street crash of 1929 further restricted global trade.As exports weakened and businesses cut production, unemployment soared. According to the UK National Archives, the number of unemployed people climbed to almost 3.5 million by 1932, with the North East of England, Scotland’s industrial lowlands and the mining valleys of Wales among the hardest-hit regions.Families faced prolonged hardship, while the government’s introduction of a means test in 1931 intensified resentment among people seeking unemployment assistance.The crisis also exposed the limits of Britain’s monetary policy. The country had returned to the gold standard in 1925, tying sterling to a fixed gold value. As economic activity contracted, deflation deepened and unemployment rose, the government faced growing pressure to defend the pound while supporting the domestic economy.The situation became critical in 1931 as investors withdrew funds from London and the Bank of England lost gold reserves. The National Archives’ record of the government’s September 20 announcement says more than £200 million had been withdrawn from the London market since mid-July. Britain suspended the gold standard the following day.The political consequences were immediate. The Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald split over how to address the financial emergency and public spending. MacDonald subsequently formed a National Government with Conservative and Liberal support, while Labour suffered a major defeat in the October 1931 election.The departure from gold eventually gave Britain greater freedom to lower interest rates and allowed sterling to depreciate, helping exporters and supporting the early stages of recovery.A research paper by economists Jason Lennard and Meredith M Paker found that leaving the gold standard reduced unemployment by 2.7 percentage points in export-intensive industries relative to less export-dependent industries.Yet recovery was uneven. Traditional industrial regions continued to experience hardship, and hunger marches brought the plight of unemployed workers into public view.Britain’s experience demonstrated how the Great Depression could undermine established industries, destabilise governments and force a major economic power to abandon a monetary system it had once considered essential to financial stability.From Wall Street to the WorldThe Great Depression proved that an economic crisis does not stop at a country’s borders. A stock market collapse in America helped fuel the rise of Hitler in Germany, deepened the misery of farmers in colonial India, pushed millions of Britons out of work, and devastated economies around the world.Yet the damage went far beyond lost jobs, failed banks and falling crop prices. Across continents, the Depression changed not only how people earned a living, but also how they viewed their governments and their future.Its legacy helped reshape the global economic order. The failure of protectionism, the instability of international finance and the inability of countries to contain the crisis through isolated national responses influenced the push for greater economic cooperation after the Second World War, including the Bretton Woods system.But the Depression’s most enduring warning is political as much as economic: when livelihoods collapse and governments appear powerless, public anger can become an opening for extremism.The crash began on Wall Street in 1929; its consequences reached farms, factories, homes and parliaments around the world, changing the course of the twentieth century.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'What is wrong with victims': CJI on digital arrest cases; calls for compensation from banks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday fumed over rising digital arrest cases and expressed shock over how educated people were getting \"arrested on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday fumed over rising digital arrest cases and expressed shock over how educated people were getting "arrested on mobile phones" despite public awareness campaigns, news reports and court orders.While hearing a suo motu case on digital arrests, CJI Surya Kant reportedly made an oral observation: "What is wrong with these victims? How are these victims being trapped like this? They can't understand this basic thing? What's the fear of arrest on mobile?""Hit the mobile on the wall and arrest goes. Something is wrong with people. God knows what is there. What kind of person are you in a democratic country if you think you are getting arrested on mobile?" a PTI report quoted the CJI.This comes after the amicus curiae in the case, NS Nappinai, said that she keeps receiving repeated inputs that while much was being done to stop digital arrests, the problem continues unabated.She told the court that a woman lost Rs 2.5 crore last week in such an incident."Something is wrong with people. God knows what is there. You are victimising yourself," the CJI retorted."We feel frustrated that all educated people are getting duped. What will you pass on to the next generation if you get digitally arrested at this age? People can go to the court's website to find if there's an order," the CJI added.'Banks must act as a protective umbrella'During the hearing, the apex court also said that banks must be held accountable for compensating victims of digital arrest scams, stressing that they should act as a “protective umbrella” for customers vulnerable to such fraud.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana questioned why unusually large withdrawals from a retired person's bank account could not trigger timely intervention to prevent the loss.The top court said it was considering directions requiring banks to compensate victims and face prosecution where digital arrest fraud occurred due to their failure to exercise due diligence."We are proposing to direct that wherever such fraud takes place, the bank will compensate the victim and suffer prosecution. It has to be done," the CJI said.Observing that banks must be made accountable to indemnify losses of victims of digital fraud, the bench said that victims of offences like digital arrests should receive compensation of at least the amount lost if the fraud is found to have resulted from a failure of due diligence by the financial institution.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: War in space? China may deploy orbital lasers to blind US satellites by late 2020s - report
articles.summary: A future war could begin by blinding an enemy before the first missile is fired.
articles.body: A future war could begin by blinding an enemy before the first missile is fired. China may be preparing to take that fight into space, with weapons capable of threatening the satellites that guide precision strikes, track enemy forces and keep modern militaries connected.According to a new report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), China could field space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, potentially expanding its ability to disrupt, damage or disable adversary satellites. The assessment warns that Beijing is also developing more powerful ground-based systems capable of threatening satellites operating in higher orbits, raising concerns over the vulnerability of US military assets in space.The DIA’s report, Challenges to Security in Space, released on October 26, warns that China is expanding its counterspace arsenal, combining directed-energy weapons with anti-satellite missiles, electronic warfare and manoeuvrable spacecraft.The report identifies the late 2020s as a potential timeline for China to field space-based directed-energy systems, although it does not confirm that such weapons are already operational in orbit.Directed-energy weapons are systems that use concentrated energy, such as high-powered lasers or high-power microwaves, to disrupt, disable or damage a target without firing conventional ammunition.In space warfare, these weapons could be used to temporarily blind a satellite’s optical sensors, interfere with its electronic systems or cause permanent damage to sensitive components.Unlike conventional anti-satellite missiles, which physically collide with and destroy their targets, directed-energy weapons can potentially affect satellites without creating large amounts of space debris. Their effectiveness, however, depends on factors such as the weapon’s power, distance from the target, targeting accuracy and the satellite’s vulnerability.The DIA said the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) considers directed-energy weapons particularly useful because they can produce both reversible and irreversible effects against satellites. Reversible attacks could include jamming satellite signals or temporarily blinding optical sensors, while more powerful systems could permanently damage sensitive components.“China and Russia will continue to pursue new and improved counterspace capabilities to exploit a perceived US and allied reliance on space-based assets,” the report concluded.Why satellites are critical in modern warfareSatellites have become a backbone of modern military operations, enabling armed forces to communicate across vast distances, track enemy movements, guide precision strikes and detect incoming missile threats. Their disruption could weaken a military’s ability to gather intelligence, coordinate forces and respond rapidly to changing battlefield conditions.Satellite-based navigation systems, such as GPS, provide positioning, navigation and timing data used by military aircraft, naval vessels, ground forces and precision-guided weapons.Surveillance satellites help identify troop concentrations, monitor naval movements and assess enemy deployments, while secure satellite communications allow commanders to exchange information with forces operating across different theatres.Satellites also play a critical role in missile warning, with specialised sensors detecting heat signatures associated with missile launches and transmitting alerts to defence networks. Losing access to these capabilities could delay threat detection and complicate military responses.For the United States, which relies heavily on space-based infrastructure to support global military operations, the threat is particularly significant.In a potential conflict over Taiwan or elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, China's ability to disrupt satellite services could complicate US force coordination and targeting.
