articles.title: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, a round loaf of bread in Herculaneum was buried under volcanic debris; it was found carbonised nearly 2,000 years later, still showing its eight segments and a baker’s stamp
articles.summary: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, a loaf of bread was still inside an oven in the Roman town of Herculaneum.
articles.body: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, a loaf of bread was still inside an oven in the Roman town of Herculaneum. The eruption buried the town, leaving the bread trapped beneath volcanic material. Nearly 2,000 years later, archaeologists found the loaf during excavations in 1930. Although it had turned black and become carbonised, the bread had survived, giving researchers a rare opportunity to examine food prepared by people living in ancient Rome.The discovery offered something that written records alone could not provide. It was an actual piece of food from the period, recovered from the place where it had been baked.The British Museum brought attention to the loaf during an exhibition on Pompeii and Herculaneum in 2013. The museum also invited Italian chef Giorgio Locatelli to prepare a version of the ancient bread. He recreated it in his London kitchen, following a recipe intended to reproduce the appearance of Roman loaves. The museum later shared the recipe and a video of the preparation process in July 2020.Information from Italy's Herculaneum Archaeological Park provides further details about the different types of bread recovered from the town, including their shapes, divisions and markings.Roman bakers cut bread into sectionsBread recovered from Herculaneum shows that bakers did not always leave the top of a loaf smooth. Many loaves were round and slightly flattened, with lines cut across the surface before baking.These lines had a practical purpose. They allowed the bread to be divided into portions more easily. One of the most common designs in the area around Mount Vesuvius had eight sections.This type of bread was called 'panis quadratus'. Its name was connected to the Latin word 'quadra', which referred to the division of bread into smaller parts. The loaf could first be divided into two halves and then into four portions, with further cuts producing eight sections.But the eight-section design was not the only one used. Archaeologists also recovered two well-preserved loaves with six sections each. One came from an area known as the House of the Brick Altar, while the other was discovered in the Palestra area.Some loaves carried marks Another detail found on Roman bread was the use of stamps. These were pressed into the dough and left marks that could remain visible after baking.The reason for these stamps becomes clearer when looking at how bread was made. In Roman towns around Mount Vesuvius, people often prepared dough in their own homes but used public ovens to bake it.With bread from different households being baked in shared facilities, markings probably helped identify who owned a loaf or where it had come from. Rectangular stamps were commonly used for this purpose.One surviving example was recovered from the House of the Brick Altar. The loaf, divided into six sections, has the letters “VM” stamped on it. The letters remain readable, although archaeologists have not established what they stood for.Chef recreated the ancient Roman loafThe British Museum's recreation offered a way to understand the preparation process. For its 2013 exhibition, chef Giorgio Locatelli made a round loaf using ingredients listed in a recipe later published by the museum.The ingredients included wholemeal or plain flour, spelt or buckwheat flour, salt, sugar, water and biga acida, a sourdough preparation.The flours were mixed before the sourdough and water were gradually added. After kneading, the dough was shaped into a ball, flattened and allowed to rise for approximately one and a half to two hours.The next stage gave the bread its distinctive appearance. A string was tightened around the outside to create a raised edge, while a knife was used to divide the top into eight sections.The museum also explained how a stamp could be added before baking. The loaf was then baked at 200 degrees Celsius for around 30 to 45 minutes.Other baked foods that survived The excavations did not reveal only large loaves. Archaeologists also found smaller flatbreads, providing further evidence of the food available in Herculaneum.Some of these were circular and resembled biscuits. They had hollowed centres and holes that may once have held strings. Their surfaces also carried geometric designs and patterns resembling plants.Three groups of these flatbreads were found stacked along the Lower Decumanus, a street in the ancient town. According to the archaeological park, they were probably displayed for sale in thermopolia, shops that sold prepared food.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: It only takes one rumour: How a small trigger can lead to a deadly stampede
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: It begins with a rumour, feeds on panic and ends in tragedy.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: It begins with a rumour, feeds on panic and ends in tragedy. A stampede can turn a celebration into chaos within minutes, leaving thousands gathered in joy struggling to find a way out. In a tightly packed crowd, even a small disturbance can have deadly consequences.A similar script played out in Kolkata on October 17. On the night of Maha Saptami during Durga Puja, pandal-hoppers gathered in large numbers at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin pandal. The crowd swelled further after a sudden spell of rain prompted people waiting outside to seek shelter, while visitors near the exit stopped moving.An announcement over the public address system warning that the pandal was about to collapse added to the panic. Investigators believe several factors contributed to the stampede, including overcrowding, narrow entry and exit points, inadequate crowd management and the misleading announcement.The crowd crush, which police said lasted around three minutes, claimed 19 lives and left at least 25 people injured.India is a country of festivals, and its massive religious gatherings also make it prone to stampedes. This year, it was Kolkata. Last year, it was Karur in Tamil Nadu and the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj. The locations change, the crowds differ, but the tragedy keeps repeating itself.This raises an important question: despite elaborate planning and dedicated crowd management teams, why do stampedes keep happening? And what can authorities do to prevent a small disturbance from turning into a disaster?The anatomy of a stampedePublic excitement soars during religious gatherings. Actual turnout often exceeds what authorities anticipate, resulting in more people entering an area than it can safely accommodate.As the crowd swells, even a small disturbance, a rumour, someone tripping and falling, a sudden power outage or even a broken barricade can lead to a situation in which people lose control of their movement.According to a 2014 report by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), titled Managing Crowd at Events and Venues of Mass Gathering: A Guide for State Government, Local Authorities, Administrators and Organizers, crowd disasters can be triggered by several factors.Structural problems such as weak temporary structures, collapsed barricades, poorly lit stairways, slippery roads and narrow entrances and exits can lead to a crowd crush.Fires, electrical failures and security scares can also turn an otherwise manageable gathering into a dangerous crush.The report explains the causes of stampedes through the "FIST" model which is an acronym for Force, Information, Space and Time. According to the model, the four factors that can contribute to a crowd disaster are the force exerted by the crowd, the information that triggers its reaction, the physical space available and the duration of the incident."The FIST circumstances namely crowd force, the information upon which the crowd acts, the physical space involved, and the time duration of the incident play a very important role resulting in either overcrowding or high desired velocity," the report says.In simple terms, when too many people are packed into a limited space, pressure builds as those behind continue moving forward while those in front are unable to move. At extreme crowd densities, people can be pushed against one another with such force that they lose control of their movements. Even those who remain standing can struggle to breathe.Deaths in such situations do not necessarily occur because someone has literally been "trampled" under the feet of others. The NDMA says compressive asphyxia, which occurs when pressure on the chest prevents a person from breathing, has historically been the most common cause of death in crowd disasters."On occasions, this has led to deaths because of crushing, suffocation, and trampling. Historically, compressive asphyxia has been the most common reason for deaths in crowd disasters," the report says.Psychology of the crowdCrowd psychology is also a factor that can contribute to a stampede-like situation. According to the NDMA report, individuals often conform their thoughts and behaviour to those of a larger group rather than acting independently."Individual behaviour in a crowd is sometimes influenced by the behaviour of others. The individuals within a crowd may act differently than if they were on their own," it says."The unlawful actions of a few people can result in larger numbers following them. Research has shown that understanding of crowd behaviour has led to community based approach to crowd control instead of force based control," the report adds.For instance, long queues at places of worship may lead some devotees to climb over fences, prompting others to follow and causing overcrowding in another area.However, crowd behaviour is not always irrational. People react to incomplete information, the movement of others and the fear of danger. In dense crowds, they may also lose the ability to control their own movement.This is why rumours and misleading announcements can be particularly dangerous. People may begin moving towards an exit without knowing what is happening elsewhere in the venue. If the exit is already congested, the sudden movement can increase pressure on those trapped in the crowd.How should police act and react?Talking to The Times of India, former Bihar director general of police Abhayanand, who handled several such gatherings during his long service, said police should refrain from using force when a crowd is already panicked during a stampede-like situation."There is always a trigger, however small. It is followed immediately thereafter by a rumour which spreads like wildfire," Abhayanand said."I haven't followed any SOP in my days. I followed two basics: The crowd has panicked. Don't increase the panic by lathi charge. If there is an individual in whom the crowd has trust and if he can be made to communicate with the crowd, its effect is magical," he added."Crowds where there is some common binding force experience stampede. Such stampedes are easier to manage," he further said.Abhayanand also recalled handling a similar situation during the funeral procession of Ranvir Sena chief Brahmeshwar Mukhiya in Patna in 2012. He said police refrained from using force against a particularly unruly gathering of supporters."The crowd was itching for a trigger, and a police lathi charge could have set things off. We restrained ourselves because the repercussions would not have been limited to the capital but could have spread across the entire state," he told TOI."Those indulging in arson wanted the police to react and resort to a lathi charge. That was precisely what they were trying to provoke, but we did not allow that trigger to be pulled," he added.His account points to the importance of police response when a crowd is already on edge. An attempt to disperse people by force can worsen the situation if it causes them to rush towards a narrow exit or move against an incoming crowd.Preparing for the unexpectedThe NDMA has also laid down guidelines on how authorities should manage crowds and respond when a stampede-like situation develops.According to the agency, the guiding principle should be to bridge the gap between demand and supply. This requires controlling the number of people entering a venue, regulating the crowd within it and managing the outflow when necessary.The NDMA recommends designated staging points through which visitors should pass, along with effective systems to count and monitor people moving through them. Multiple routes should be encouraged to prevent bottlenecks and facilitate the movement of vulnerable groups.Crowd management also requires authorities to anticipate disturbances without allowing their response to trigger a larger crisis."Such miscreants should be immediately quarantined and removed. Action should be taken immediately with tact and firmness, without inviting undue attention from the general public, which may be there if force is used," it says."Inappropriate or poorly managed control procedures may precipitate crowd incidents rather than preventing them. For example, police reacting to a group of unruly people may chase them in a direction opposite to the incoming crowd, which may create a collision, and hence a disaster. Special attention should also be given to the border of the venue and the floating crowd moving there because the mischief is usually caused at such places," it adds.The agency also recommends "input control" by restricting or staggering entry to prevent overcrowding. Authorities must be able to regulate, slow or temporarily stop the inflow when a venue reaches its safe capacity.This also means keeping entry and exit routes clear, ensuring that people leaving a venue do not collide with those entering, and monitoring areas where crowds tend to gather or stop moving.Communication is another important part of crowd management. The NDMA says a lack of reliable information can cause people to panic or change direction, leading to dangerous crowd movements."Communicating with visitors and providing them with the correct information is a very critical factor in all situations," the report says, stressing that communication is essential during normal operations, emergencies and recovery.The Kolkata tragedy showed how quickly things can go wrong when these safeguards fail. Police said the crowd had become congested near the exit during the rain, even as the entry point remained open. The misleading announcement about the pandal collapsing is believed to have added to the pressure, although investigators are still examining the exact sequence of events.Ultimately, effective crowd management lies in anticipating pressure, regulating movement and ensuring that a small trigger does not turn into an uncontrollable chain of events. The challenge is not just to prepare for the thousands expected to attend an event, but also to recognise when a gathering is becoming unsafe and act before it is too late.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Hyderabad developer building a 150-acre residential project faced losing around 800 mango trees to a link road, so he bought another plot and spent six to eight months moving the trees instead of cutting them down
articles.summary: When a link road threatened around 800 mango trees on a 150-acre residential project in Hyderabad, developer Ashwin Rao faced a difficult choice: allow
articles.body: When a link road threatened around 800 mango trees on a 150-acre residential project in Hyderabad, developer Ashwin Rao faced a difficult choice: allow the trees to be cut or find a way to preserve them. He chose the latter, bought another plot of land and arranged to move the trees. The process took six to eight months.As reported by The Indian Express, Rao’s decision was influenced by an earlier experience in 2015, when a nearly 100-year-old banyan tree in Zaheerabad faced removal. With help from the Vata Foundation, an organisation that works to protect and relocate trees, he moved the tree to vacant land he owned. That experience taught him that relocating a mature tree involves more than digging it out and planting it elsewhere. Its roots, orientation and growing conditions must also be considered.Why moving mature trees is not as simple as planting saplingsWhen development projects require trees to be removed, compensatory plantation is often used to offset the loss. But planting new saplings does not immediately replace the benefits of mature trees, which have spent years growing and storing carbon. As reported by The Indian Express, tree translocation, uprooting a tree and replanting it at another location is one alternative when preserving a tree in its original place is not possible. However, the process is technically demanding, and survival is not guaranteed.The Vata Foundation, which assisted Rao with the banyan tree, has been involved in relocating mature trees since 2015. According to the foundation’s official website, its work includes identifying trees threatened by development, finding suitable locations and helping arrange their relocation.The organisation's work highlights why preparation matters. Trees must be handled carefully during uprooting and transport, and they need appropriate conditions and continued care after being replanted. Rao’s experience with the banyan tree also highlighted the importance of timing. The 2015 relocation was carried out during the monsoon, when, he said, the “chances of survival of translocated trees are the highest”. The same principle informed the later effort to move the mango trees.How the foundation helps trees find new homesVata Foundation founder Uday Krishna began exploring alternatives to tree felling after a construction project in Hyderabad in 2010 required 45 trees to be cut. During a later foot-overbridge project, he arranged to move 16 trees instead. Thirteen survived. That experience also exposed a gap in how compensatory planting was monitored. Krishna observed that after permission was granted to remove trees for development, there was often little follow-up on whether replacement saplings survived.The foundation subsequently developed a tree-adoption model. Some adopters provide both land and funds, while others offer land where trees can be replanted. According to Krishna, the foundation has helped more than 17,500 trees find new homes since 2015, drawing on a network of around 8,000 people across the country.The foundation’s work also shows why moving mature trees cannot be treated as a guaranteed solution. In 2018, volunteers found two banyan trees, each more than 100 years old, that had been uprooted and left beside a road. A school in Hyderabad agreed to adopt them, and a fourth-grade girl in the United States raised around Rs 95,000 towards the relocation.The operation faced several problems. The equipment was inadequate, the truck transporting the trees broke down, and the trees were moved around 10 days after they had been uprooted. Only one survived.Another rescue had a different outcome. In 2017, a Jungle Jalebi tree at Government Girls High School in Nagarkurnool fell during a storm but continued bearing fruit. The school's former principal, Yashodha, resisted its removal for almost two-and-a-half months. After learning about the tree, Krishna offered to help. On July 28, 2017, his team used a single JCB to set it upright again. The schoolgirls have since held a festival for the tree every year on that date.Why conservationists say relocation should be the last resortTree translocation has also been considered for larger infrastructure projects. Vata Foundation partnered with the Indian Navy on a project involving thousands of mature trees in the Damagundam Reserve Forest in Telangana, where a Very Low Frequency radar communication station is planned. The project involves diversion of forest land and tree felling.The wider challenge is not simply how many trees are planted or moved, but whether they survive and continue to provide ecological benefits. The Vata Foundation’s work reflects the importance of finding suitable sites and arranging care after relocation, rather than treating the act of planting as the end of the process.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1962, the Willis family moved onto farmland in Rowlett, Texas; 64 years later the city wants their four-generation home for a road project, and the family says the city's offer is $150,000 short
articles.summary: A home that has remained in a family for generations is now at the centre of a property dispute in Rowlett, Texas, as the city seeks to acquire it for a
articles.body: A home that has remained in a family for generations is now at the centre of a property dispute in Rowlett, Texas, as the city seeks to acquire it for a road improvement project. The Willis family moved to the area in 1962, when the surrounding land was largely farmland. More than six decades later, the family says the city's compensation offer does not reflect the value of the property it is being asked to leave. A CBS News Texas report published on October 27, 2026, said the city's final offer was $429,000, which the family rejected. The dispute centres on the planned widening of Chiesa Road and the city's use of eminent domain to obtain land for public infrastructure.A family home dating back to 1962Roy Willis told CBS News Texas that his family moved to the property when the surrounding area was undeveloped, with cotton fields and cornfields occupying much of the land. The home, near Lake Ray Hubbard and Chiesa Road, has since become a longstanding family residence spanning four generations. Willis said he, his father and his brother built the house. The property has significance beyond its monetary value because it represents decades of family history and remains home to relatives.The dispute has also affected his brother, Timothy Willis, who is disabled and lives on a fixed income. In its October 26 report, Texas Metro News quoted Timothy expressing sadness about the prospect of losing the family home. For the family, therefore, the issue is not simply the sale of a property. It is the possible loss of a place connected to their family history and present living arrangements.Why the city wants the propertyThe proposed acquisition is part of Rowlett's Chiesa Road improvement plans. The city says the existing road has become too narrow to accommodate traffic flow and plans to widen it. CBS News Texas reported that the project would require the city to acquire private land and that the Willis house is among the properties affected. City council records provide further context for the wider road scheme. Rowlett's plans call for a four-lane divided roadway within a 90-foot right-of-way along the Chiesa Road corridor between Dalrock Road and Miller Road. The city plans to acquire private land to make room for the road improvements.In a separate update published on July 31, 2026, the city outlined reconstruction work on Chiesa Road between Miller Road and State Highway 66/Rowlett Road. That work focuses on restoring the road's original design grade and improving its condition. The city's wider road plans and the reconstruction work provide infrastructure context, although they should not be treated as identical project phases.The dispute over compensationThe central disagreement concerns how much the family should receive for its property. CBS News Texas reported that a final letter from the city contained an offer of $429,000, which the Willis family declined. Texas Metro News reported that the family believes the offer falls $150,000 short of the amount it is seeking. The family argues that the valuation does not adequately account for the property's worth, pointing to development taking place nearby. Roy Willis told CBS News Texas that a major development within approximately 1,000 feet of the property should be considered when determining appropriate compensation.The family has also raised concerns about the impact of the road project on its land. According to CBS News Texas, the Willises believe the planned acquisition would cut their property in half, while the city intends to remove the house to make way for the public road expansion. However, the $150,000 difference reflects the family's position in the compensation dispute. It should not be interpreted as an independently established shortfall in market value. Determining whether an offer is fair requires consideration of the property's valuation and the circumstances of the acquisition.What eminent domain meansThe dispute involves eminent domain, the legal authority that allows government entities to acquire private property for public use, subject to applicable legal requirements and compensation rules. Texas Metro News quoted eminent domain attorney Clint Schumacher of Dawson & Sodd PLLC, who was not involved in the Willis case, explaining fair market value as the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller when neither is compelled to complete the transaction.That distinction is important in disputes involving compulsory acquisitions. A property owner's attachment to a home may be profound, but compensation negotiations generally focus on legally relevant valuation considerations rather than sentimental value alone. The family can dispute the proposed compensation through the applicable legal process. The city of Rowlett said it does not comment on pending or anticipated litigation, including matters that may involve eminent domain proceedings. Texas Metro News reported that the family had been given a deadline to accept the offer and that the city council was expected to discuss in executive session whether to pursue an eminent domain lawsuit. The reports do not establish that a lawsuit has been filed or that a court has ruled on the compensation.A road project with personal consequencesRowlett's plan reflects the infrastructure demands of a growing community, but for the Willis family, the proposed acquisition threatens a home built through generations of family effort. The disagreement now centres on whether the city and the family can reach an acceptable compensation agreement or whether the dispute will proceed through the legal system. For a family that has lived on the property since 1962, the proposed road expansion represents more than a change to the local landscape. It could mean leaving a home that has shaped family life for 64 years. The final outcome will depend on the negotiations and any subsequent legal proceedings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why this British woman spent years collecting 4,550 My Little Pony items after her parents refused to buy her a horse
articles.summary: Miranda Worby’s childhood wish for a real horse took an unexpected turn when her parents refused to buy her one.
articles.body: Miranda Worby’s childhood wish for a real horse took an unexpected turn when her parents refused to buy her one. Instead, she found comfort in My Little Pony, the colourful toy ponies that eventually became the centre of a lifelong passion. Decades later, the British collector amassed 4,550 pieces of My Little Pony memorabilia, earning a Guinness World Records title for the largest collection of its kind. What began as a childhood interest has grown into an extraordinary collection that fills her home and continues to expand.A childhood wish for a horse lead to 4,550 My Little Pony itemsAccording to Guinness World Records, Worby’s collection began with a pink pony named Snowflake, which she still owns. Her fascination with the toys started when she was young, offering an alternative to the real horse she had hoped to have.In February 2024, ITV News Anglia reported that Worby received her first My Little Pony at the age of four. The toys appealed to her because they came in different colours and designs, with so many characters to discover.That variety helped turn a childhood toy into a lasting interest. Rather than losing enthusiasm as she grew older, Worby became increasingly interested in finding more figures and related merchandise. Her collection eventually reached a scale that few fans could imagine, with thousands of items gathered over several decades.The collection grew beyond toys into a remarkable archiveAs reported by Guinness World Records in September 2026, Worby’s collection includes much more than the familiar plastic ponies. Her shelves contain classic figures alongside backpacks, mugs, clothing, make-up and other merchandise inspired by the franchise.The scale of the collection became increasingly difficult to manage. By 2018, Worby had moved to a larger house so she could display her growing assortment. ITV News Anglia reported that she shared the Lowestoft, Suffolk, home with her partner, Ian, and had dedicated an entire room to the collection.Even that additional space was not enough to accommodate everything. Some items were displayed at home while a comparable amount remained in storage. The couple had effectively run out of room, although Worby had no intention of stopping her search for new additions.Her collection also came with a significant financial commitment. ITV reported that she had spent thousands of pounds on pony-related items over the years, building what she believed was among the largest collections in the UK.A rare arcade ride became one of her unique acquisitionAmong Worby’s most unusual possessions is a My Little Pony arcade ride from the 1990s. The acquisition demonstrated how her enthusiasm extended beyond collecting small figures to preserving larger pieces of merchandise associated with the franchise.According to Guinness World Records, getting the ride home proved more complicated than she had expected. She had not fully appreciated its size when arranging to collect it. The previous owner had kept it in a child’s bedroom, but getting it out had required removing the bungalow’s front door.Worby recalled having to sit in the car’s footwell during the journey home because the ride took up so much space. The episode offered a glimpse of the practical challenges that can accompany collecting unusual objects, particularly when they were never designed for easy transport or long-term storage.The ride has also connected her collection with other enthusiasts. Guinness World Records reported that people had sent Worby photographs of themselves enjoying similar arcade rides during their own childhoods. Her acquisition serves as a reminder of a toy era that many people remember fondly.Rare finds and childhood memories keep the search aliveAlthough the collection contains thousands of objects, some pieces carry more personal meaning than others. Guinness World Records reported that Worby’s favourite is the Megan and Sundance figure set, which she received for her 5th birthday. Its value comes from the memories attached to it and the hours she spent playing with it as a child.Another prized possession is Fireball, a pony manufactured in Thailand. Worby considers it her rarest item, with only 2 examples believed to exist.Finding pieces like these can require considerable effort. According to Guinness World Records, she has travelled two hours to collect a particularly desirable item, while also asking people living in different parts of the UK to pick up ponies on her behalf. She has even found herself competing against other buyers at her local auction house.Her collection has also become distinctive for a detail that might surprise people unfamiliar with the toys. Worby says the figures retain their individual smells, a feature that inspired her social media username, @sniffingplasticponies. For her, the appeal goes beyond their appearance and includes the sensory details associated with the toys.A record-breaking collection that is still unfinishedThe record has not marked the end of her collecting. Guinness World Records reported that she is still searching for a Generation One pony called Bon Bon, a character associated with the 1990s cartoon. Despite the size of her collection, this particular item has continued to elude her.Worby believes the franchise remains popular because of its nostalgic appeal and the way different generations discover it through family members. Its straightforward concept and colourful characters offer a familiar attraction for children and adults alike.The friendships formed through collecting have become another part of the experience. Her interest has helped her meet people who share her enthusiasm. She has also encouraged collectors not to feel embarrassed about their hobbies, pointing out that others are likely to appreciate the same things.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.summary: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.
articles.body:
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.

The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.

While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.

Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.

Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.

It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.

It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."

In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".

The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.

Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.

This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.

Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.

In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.

Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.

The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".

"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.

Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.

Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.

Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.

Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.

"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."

Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.

A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.

Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.

"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".

Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.

"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.

"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title: Mini-gardens for bees on Peterborough bus stop roofs approved
articles.summary: Living Roofs aimed at boosting biodiversity in urban areas will be installed under a new bus stop contract.
articles.body:
Plans to introduce "bee bus stops" aimed to boost biodiversity in urban areas have been approved for Peterborough.

Peterborough City Council said 34 bus stops could include Living Roofs, mini-gardens planted on top of bus shelters that are made up of wildflowers and other vegetation.

The initiative was included in its new plan for the city's bus stops, which will also see "comfortable seating" replace existing perch seats.

At a meeting of the cabinet on Tuesday, the plans were discussed and approved.

The council will award a new contract to Bauer Media Outdoor UK to manage the city's bus stops.

The agreement includes the company providing the council with an annual income of £140,000 from the sale of advertising space, plus 2.5% of its quarterly gross revenue.

The contract is expected to run for a minimum of 10 years, with options to extend it, and could provide the authority with £2.8m over 20 years.

There are more than 350 Living Roofs across the UK, including in Birmingham, Glasgow and Northampton.

Chris Wiggin, the council's Liberal Democrat cabinet member for environment, said: "We need to do everything we can to support biodiversity and support bees and other pollinators because without those there is no other life, so I'm very happy to see these [plans] come forward."

Other planned changes to the city's bus stops include providing up-to-date passenger information and installing digital advertising screens at most bus stops.

articles.title: A Texas grandmother's safe-deposit box sparked a family fight over alleged $400,000 cash, an eight-carat diamond and gold coins; after a jury awarded her niece $796,906, an October 27 appeals court overturned it
articles.summary: A Texas woman's decision to share access to her bank safe-deposit box with her niece led to a family dispute involving claims of $400,000 in cash, an
articles.body: A Texas woman's decision to share access to her bank safe-deposit box with her niece led to a family dispute involving claims of $400,000 in cash, an eight-carat diamond ring and gold coins.According to the details of the case available on Justia, the disagreement began after Joyce Kezhaya died in August 2019, when her grandson emptied the box and reported finding only $16,000. Her niece later took him to court and won nearly $797,000 in damages. However, on Tuesday, a Texas appeals court overturned the award, ruling that she had failed to make her claim through the required process before her aunt's estate was settled.At the centre of the case was a question that remained unresolved even after years of legal proceedings: what was actually inside the bank box? Kezhaya's grandson, Nathanial Reggish, maintained that it contained $16,000, a family Bible and a few other belongings. But one of Kezhaya's daughters told the court that she had seen a much larger amount of cash, along with valuable jewellery and gold coins.The woman who brought the case, Kezhaya Stephens, was Kezhaya's niece. She had been given access to the box in May 2015, shortly after her aunt opened it. The bank's agreement allowed either woman to use the box independently. Yet, according to the case document, Stephens had never opened it herself. She did not have a key and had no direct knowledge of what her aunt had stored there.What happened after grandmother's death?Kezhaya had four children Jerry, Lexus, Valana and Tommy. In January 2019, after developing health problems, she prepared a will appointing her grandson Reggish, Valana's son, to manage her estate. According to testimony presented during the trial, Lexus and Valana were the only beneficiaries named in the will.Her condition worsened later that year, and she was admitted to hospital in July. Reggish applied to become her temporary guardian, a request the court approved on August 7, 2019. Kezhaya died later that day.The following day, Reggish visited the bank with his mother, Valana. They opened the safe-deposit box and took away its contents. Lexus had been asked to come along but stayed outside the bank. Since the removal was not recorded on video, the court later had to rely on accounts given by family members.Reggish said he found $16,000 in cash and arranged for the money to be deposited in a trust account. The amount was subsequently recorded among Kezhaya's estate assets.Meanwhile, Lexus told the jury that she had seen the items from the box afterwards in a hotel room. She described 40 bundles of cash containing $10,000 each, besides an eight-carat diamond ring and numerous gold coins. Her account suggested that the cash alone totalled $400,000.Niece takes her cousin to courtStephens said she had planned to visit the bank after her aunt's death to open the box as a last goodbye. Instead, she learnt that Reggish and Valana had already taken everything out.Although her name was on the bank agreement, Stephens acknowledged that she had never seen the contents herself. Her belief about what the box held came from what other people had told her. She initially sought $382,000.She eventually sued Reggish and Valana, accusing them of wrongfully taking property, fraud, and conspiracy. Her case was based on her claim that the contents belonged to her rather than forming part of her aunt's estate.Meanwhile, Kezhaya's children were settling the inheritance. They reached an agreement on how the estate would be divided, and the court approved it in March 2021. The settlement included the $16,000 that Reggish had reported finding in the bank box. Reggish himself received no share of the estate.Stephens's separate case continued even after the inheritance proceedings ended. In June 2023, the court decided to hear her claims against Reggish separately from those against Valana.A jury subsequently sided with Stephens, and the trial court ordered Reggish to pay her $796,905.89. But he appealed, questioning both the evidence of ownership and the way she had pursued her claim.Appeals court cancels $796,906 awardThe appeals court did not attempt to settle the competing accounts of what was inside the box. Instead, it examined whether Stephens had followed the legal process required to claim property connected to her aunt's estate.Reggish argued that any such claim should have been made before the estate was closed. Stephens maintained that she had sued him as an individual, not as the person managing the inheritance, and that the rules governing claims against an estate therefore did not apply.The judges rejected that distinction. They found that Reggish had accessed the box while acting in his official capacity as Kezhaya's temporary guardian. The money he reported finding had also been included in the estate and distributed through the inheritance proceedings.The court said Stephens should have formally presented her claim to the estate's representative or the court clerk before the estate was closed. There was no evidence that she had taken either step. She had also not challenged Reggish's authority to access the box or the distribution of its contents during those proceedings.As a result, the appeals court ruled that her claim against Reggish could not succeed under the Texas Estates Code. It cancelled the earlier award and ordered that Stephens receive nothing from her lawsuit against him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Bokaro readies tight security for JTET on Nov 1: 46,181 candidates at 72 centres, cyber monitoring, GPS-tracked paper transport, device ban and screening.
articles.body: Bokaro: A total of 46,181 candidates are set to appear across 72 centres in Bokaro district for the Jharkhand Teachers Eligibility Test (JTET) scheduled to take place in the state on Nov 1, officials said on Thursday during a joint briefing by deputy commissioner Ajay Nath Jha and SP Nathu Singh Meena with the centre superintendents, magistrates and police officers for ensuring a free and fair examination.Jha said, “Maintaining the integrity and transparency of the examination is the key priority and anyone showing laxity will be taken to task. Everyone must be vigilant to curb any attempts to leak question papers and fraudsters seeking to cheat candidates by circulating fake papers.”Meena said, “Cyber cell and social media monitoring team would keep a close watch on misleading information. A proper plan has been readied to ensure proper screening of candidates, bar unauthorised entry, and secure transportation of question papers under police escort. Vehicles carrying question papers will be monitored through GPS.”The examination will be conducted in two shifts. The first shift, from 9.30 am to noon, will cater to 31,326 candidates appearing for Classes VI to VIII, while 14,855 candidates seeking eligibility for Classes I to V will take the test from 2 pm to 4.30 pm.The administration has imposed strict restrictions on electronic devices and other prohibited items at examination centres for the JTET-2026. Candidates must undergo mandatory screening, while invigilators must deposit their mobile phones before entering examination rooms. articles.summary: RAJKOT: A man was booked for allegedly setting his neighbour’s car on fire in Morbi after becoming irritated by the vehicle’s parking sensor alerts,
articles.body: RAJKOT: A man was booked for allegedly setting his neighbour’s car on fire in Morbi after becoming irritated by the vehicle’s parking sensor alerts, police said. The fire caused damage estimated at Rs 3.5 lakh to the car owned by a woman advocate.Morbi City ‘A’ Division police have registered a case against the accused, identified as Shikhar Jayeshbhai Gohel, for allegedly pouring an inflammable substance on the car and setting it ablaze.The incident came to light after CCTV footage showing the alleged act went viral.The footage shows a man approaching the parked car with what appears to be a container of inflammable liquid. He pours the liquid over the vehicle, takes out a matchbox and sets it on fire. Within moments, flames begin to engulf the car.The man then appears to take out his mobile phone and record the burning vehicle instead of leaving the scene. The footage subsequently shows him unlocking another car parked across the street. He returns towards the burning vehicle before getting into the other car and driving away a few minutes later.The timestamp visible in the footage reads 4.44pm on October 28.According to the complaint, Pushpa Bhatt, a practising advocate residing on Ravapar Road, had parked her car near the residence of fellow advocate Mahidhar Dave on Vaghpara Street No. 17 around 2 pm on Wednesday after returning from work.At around 5pm, Dave called Bhatt to inform her that her car had caught fire outside his house. Bhatt and her husband rushed to the spot and found the bonnet engulfed in flames, while local residents were trying to douse the fire.Emergency services and the fire brigade were alerted, and firefighters eventually brought the blaze under control. The fire gutted almost the entire vehicle, including the cabin and engine compartment, leaving only the rear boot area relatively unaffected.The alleged act came to light when Dave reviewed CCTV footage recorded by a camera installed outside his residence. The footage purportedly showed their neighbour, Gohel, pouring a flammable substance over the car and setting it on fire.Speaking to The Times of India, police inspector Y B Jadeja said the complainant and the accused were neighbours and had an ongoing dispute over parking.“According to preliminary information, the car was being parked near the accused’s residence, and he used to get irritated by the vehicle’s parking sensors, which would beep repeatedly,” Jadeja said.Based on Bhatt’s complaint, Morbi City ‘A’ Division police booked Gohel under Sections 326(f) and 324(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Rajkot | Silver Rate in Rajkot | Bank Holidays in Rajkot | Public Holidays in Rajkot | Rajkot AQI | Weather in Rajkot | Petrol Price in Rajkot | Diesel Price in Rajkot | CNG Price in Rajkot | LPG Price in RajkotStay updated with the latest Rajkot news. articles.title: Husband surrenders in advocate death case, levels allegations against in-laws in video
articles.summary: Jharkhand HC advocate Anushka Chakraborty death: husband Kushagra Rudra surrenders in Hazaribag, denies dowry charges in video; police seek custody.
articles.body: Hazaribag: Kushagra Rudra (31), the husband of deceased Jharkhand high court advocate Anushka Chakraborty (28) and a key accused in her death, surrendered before the Chief Judicial Magistrate’s court in Hazaribag on Thursday. Police said they would seek his remand for custodial interrogation.Anushka was found hanging inside her apartment in Hazaribag on Oct 22. Her family subsequently accused Rudra and his relatives of dowry-related harassment and murder. The case later came before the Jharkhand high court, which directed that the investigation be supervised by an officer of DSP rank.Hours before surrendering, Rudra released a video on social media denying all allegations against him and his family. In the video, he alleged that Anushka’s father had repeatedly interfered in his business affairs and pressured him to appoint him as a director in his company. He further claimed that his in-laws had made financial demands and that he had spent a substantial amount on their behalf.Rudra also alleged that marital discord arose over Anushka’s alleged closeness to a woman advocate during her stay in Ranchi. He claimed that the advocate had influenced Anushka’s personal and career decisions. He further alleged that Anushka had undergone an abortion in Ranchi and linked it to advice she had allegedly received to focus on her legal career before starting a family.The allegations made in the video have not been independently verified. No response from those named in the video was immediately available.Sadar SDPO Rupesh Kumar Singh confirmed Rudra’s surrender and said police had moved the court seeking his custody for questioning. An SIT constituted by Hazaribag SP Aman Kumar is probing the case. Police said all allegations and counter-allegations were being examined as part of the investigation.Anushka and Kushagra got married in 2024 and lived in Hazaribag city. After she began practising at the Jharkhand high court in 2025, she moved to a rented flat in Ranchi where her husband used to visit her.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Mystery celebrity in London says he will 'kill himself' if sexual misconduct allegations against him are made public
articles.summary: A celebrity whose name has been kept under wraps has approached the High Court in London against news organizations attempting to publish sexual
articles.body: A celebrity whose name has been kept under wraps has approached the High Court in London against news organizations attempting to publish sexual misconduct allegations against him. His lawyers recently told the court that he denied the allegations of abusing his power and position as a celebrity to "contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them". They said the celebrity is "highly likely" to attempt suicide. The lawyers sought an injunction against Guardian News and Media and ITN. The news organizations backed their rights to publish their articles, arguing that there was no legitimate basis to "restrain the publication of public interest journalism". They said the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be lowered through treatment. The news outlets told the court that the allegations against the celebrity, referred to as PPT, involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts.Very little has come to the public so far. The celebrity is male and is being represented by Sara Mansoori KC. She told the court that her client had first attempted to kill himself in May when the Guardian and ITN contacted him to give him the chance to respond to the allegations. On that very afternoon, he was admitted to hospital.PPT made a second attempt in July, Mansoori told the court."They (the media outlets) say they have a duty to publish because it's substantially in the public interest, but their assessment of the public interest is wrong. A newspaper does not have the right to publish information at the cost of an individual being killed or maimed," Mansoori argued."The only way (publication) wouldn't be fatal is if the claimant is locked up and prevented from taking his own life," she added.PPT's lawyers said that publication of the claims would breach his right to life and subject him to inhumane or degrading treatment under Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.Gavin Millar KC, who is representing the media outlets, described the claims as "unprecedented". "'His contention is that if the allegations are published he will commit suicide, and the state's duty requires this court to restrain (the outlets) from publishing them. Insofar as the state owes a duty to PPT, it is discharged by NHS mental health services and practitioners. There is a strong public interest in publishing these allegations which are credible and which (the outlets) believe to be true," Miller argued.As the hearing continues, the judge asked the public to refrain from speculating who the celebrity could be.(If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, a global list of helplines is available at blog.opencounseling.com/suicide-hotlines/)You use AI every day.
